newsitem.title: FRANCE: French ex-minister blames EU neighbours on terrorism.
newsitem.headline: French ex-minister blames EU neighbours on terrorism.

text.p: Former French Interior Minister Charles Pasqua accused Belgium, Germany and Britain on Sunday of offering immunity to Islamic guerrilla groups in exchange for promises not to operate on their territories.

Pasqua, interior minister until last year, levelled the accusation as a fourth person died from the bombing of a Paris commuter train on Tuesday. He was identified as student Yunes Nait Slimane, 28, the second Moroccan killed in the attack.
Pasqua's comments came on the eve of the trial of 34 Moslem fundamentalists accused of backing a Moroccan guerrilla group amid fears the case could prompt further bomb attacks.

No formal link has been established between the two cases. But several anonymous telephone calls to newspapers and radios after Tuesday's bombing said there would be further attacks if France did not release Moslem fundamentalists held in its jails.
Commenting on suspicions Islamic fundamentalists were to blame for the latest bomb attack, Pasqua said:

"It is clear that a certain number of countries have agreements of a sort with Islamic terrorist organisations," he told TF1 television. "Don't do anything on our soil and we'll let you through (our borders,)" Pasqua said were the terms.

Pasqua, a member of President Jacques Chirac's Rally for the Republic neo-Gaullist party, said: "Those in charge of (fighting terrorism) know and everyone knows that this is the case in Belgium and everyone knows that it is the case in Germany.
"As far as Britain is concerned, everyone knows that the leaders of all the radical Islamic fundamentalist movements are there, all of them," he said.

Pasqua, interior minister from 1986-1988 and 1993-1995, was deeply involved in countering Islamic groups when in office, and ordered the December 1994 storming of an airliner hijacked by Algerian fundamentalists who shot dead three passengers.

Algeria's Armed Islamic Group (GIA), claiming responsibility for a wave of bomb attacks in which eight people died and 160 were injured in France last year, said they were avenging the four hijackers who were killed by police in the operation.
Pasqua said France faced the threat of Islamic terrorism because the country had five million Moslems "including 50,000 fundamentalists of whom about 2,000 are real radicals".

No one has claimed responsibility for Tuesday's blast, in which 94 people were injured. But French newspapers said a list of suspects Paris sent to other European countries was thought to be composed solely of Islamic activists.

Pasqua said it was unfortunate the bulk of French Moslems might suffer from suspicions due to the actions of a few, but called on the government to instantly expel foreign Moslem religious leaders who preached violence.
He agreed however that many Moslems could not be expelled because they were children of North African immigrants who automatically became French nationals by being born in France.
Coincidentally, the trial was set to open on Monday of 34 fundamentalists, mostly French-born children of Arab immigrants.
They were recruited by Morocco's outlawed Islamic Youth Movement whose aim was to overthrow King Hassan and create an Islamic regime in the North African country, prosecutors say.
Members of the group were sent for weapons training aboard, including to Afganistan and carried out hold-ups in France to finance their activities, prosecutors say.
